title: The new covenant (Hebrews 8)
hookLine: Hebrews quotes Jeremiah: I will write my laws on their hearts
tomorrow: if you can pray anywhere, why does Hebrews care who shows up?

lines: A LESSON QUOTING NO MORE LESSONS.
cards: Nobody needs a tutorial for their best friend's laugh, or the words to a song they grew up on. Some things you know so well you can't remember learning them. Keep that in mind, because Hebrews has an odd moment.
It's a long, careful lesson, argument after argument.

And in the middle of it, the writer quotes a promise that sounds like it would put every teacher out of work: "And they shall not teach every man his neighbour, and every man his brother, saying, Know the Lord: for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest."
Why would a teaching letter quote that?

teach.b: The promise comes from the prophet Jeremiah, and Hebrews quotes it at length. It opens: "Behold, the days come, saith the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah."
A covenant is a binding promise between two parties.

Then the clue to the puzzle, where this one is kept: "I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts: and I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people." There's the answer.
The knowing promised here isn't a set of facts you could look up. It's the way you know a voice, or a person. Teaching doesn't vanish.
It moves inside, until knowing and wanting start to line up. And under it all, mercy: "their sins and their iniquities will I remember no more."
Two readings meet here, and this lesson ranks neither.

Jeremiah spoke these words to the house of Israel and the house of Judah, and Jewish readers read them within Israel's own covenant. The writer of Hebrews reads them through Jesus, the high priest of the chapters before.
The detail to tell a friend tonight: the same promise lives in two Bibles, in Jeremiah's own pages and again, quoted, in Hebrews.

how: Christians read Hebrews 8 and Jeremiah 31 in worship and study, and at communion some churches repeat Jesus' words about the cup of the new covenant.

o: God's promise to write his laws on people's hearts
a fresh set of rules carved on new stone tablets
a contract signed when someone joins a church

games.q: the promise in Hebrews 8 — tap the pairs.
p: a binding promise between two parties
into the mind, written in hearts

s: the new covenant is first promised in the New Testament
Jeremiah promised it; Hebrews quotes him at length.
know the Lord here means knowing facts about God
it's the knowing of a person, written in the heart, from the least to the greatest.
Jewish and Christian readers both treasure Jeremiah's promise
Jewish readers read it within Israel's covenant; Hebrews reads it through Jesus.

games.q: your little cousin memorized a verse to win a sticker at church, then forgot it a week later. your aunt sighs: what's the point? what does Hebrews 8's promise point toward?
o: stop memorizing; the heart doesn't need words.
knowing that lives inside, not recited for a prize.
more drills, until the recall is perfect.
games.why: I will write them in their hearts: the promise is knowing God the way you know a person, which words learned by heart can help, not replace.

practice: Say one short line you know by heart, out loud and slowly: a verse, a grace before meals, something a grandparent always said. Notice that you didn't need a page to find it.
Then say it once more, softer, and let the quiet after it be the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: The new covenant. A promise from Jeremiah, quoted in Hebrews eight: laws put into the mind and written on the heart.

orig.note: Greek: covenant; the word in Hebrews 8 for the covenant Jeremiah promised.

carryVoice: Keep this one: on their hearts, not on stone and not on a screen. Until tomorrow.
